content: Dexlansoprazole is a medication used to treat conditions caused by excessive stomach acid, such as heartburn, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and erosive esophagitis (EE). It works by reducing the amount of acid produced in the stomach. It is available in delayed-release oral capsules of 30 mg and 60 mg, marketed under brand names like Dexilant and Kapidex, as well as in generic forms. Important Usage Instructions: Dexlansoprazole should only be taken if prescribed by a healthcare provider and must be used exactly as directed. Do not share this medication with others, even if they have similar symptoms, as it may harm them. The capsules should not be chewed, cut, or crushed. They can be taken with or without food. If swallowing the capsule is difficult, it can be opened, and the contents sprinkled on one tablespoon of applesauce, which should be swallowed immediately without mixing with other foods. If administered through a nasogastric (NG) tube, follow the specific instructions provided by your healthcare provider. This medication is not intended for immediate relief of heartburn, as it may take 1 to 4 days to achieve its full effect. Precautions: Keep this medication out of reach of children. Do not use dexlansoprazole if you are allergic to it, other proton pump inhibitors, or any of its ingredients. Consult your pharmacist for a complete list of ingredients. Inform your healthcare provider about all your current and past health conditions, including low levels of potassium, magnesium, calcium, or sodium in the blood, as well as any liver problems. Discuss all medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and supplements you are taking to avoid potential interactions. This includes prescription and over-the-counter (OTC) drugs. Special Considerations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: It is not known if dexlansoprazole affects pregnancy or passes into breast milk. Inform your healthcare provider if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Children Under 2 Years: This medication may pose a higher risk of side effects in children under 2 years of age. Consult your healthcare provider about the risks. Drug Interactions: Dexlansoprazole may interact with certain medications, such as methotrexate, digoxin, warfarin, tacrolimus, antiretroviral drugs (e.g., rilpivirine, nelfinavir, saquinavir), St. John’s Wort, and rifampin. These interactions can alter the effectiveness of dexlansoprazole or the other medications. Always inform your healthcare provider about all medications you are taking. There are no known interactions between dexlansoprazole and foods or drinks, but the effects of alcohol on this medication are unclear. Side Effects: Common Side Effects: These include diarrhea, stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, gas, cold symptoms, sore throat, and headache (especially in children aged 12 to 17). Contact your healthcare provider if these symptoms persist or worsen. Serious Side Effects: These include: Kidney Problems: Acute interstitial nephritis may occur. Seek immediate medical attention if you notice decreased urine output or blood in your urine. Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhea: Overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) in the gut can cause watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in stool, severe stomach cramps, or fever. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if these symptoms occur. Severe Skin Reactions: Conditions like Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) or Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) can cause painful red or purple skin, peeling, blisters, or watery eyes. Stop the medication and seek emergency care if these symptoms develop. Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS): This rare allergic reaction can affect multiple organs, including the liver, kidneys, and heart. Symptoms include rash, fever, swollen lymph nodes, shortness of breath, swelling in the legs, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Stop the medication and seek immediate medical attention. Lupus: Dexlansoprazole may trigger or worsen lupus, an autoimmune disorder. Report new or worsening joint pain or a rash on your arms or cheeks to your healthcare provider. Vitamin B12 Deficiency: Long-term use (3 years or more) may reduce vitamin B12 absorption, leading to symptoms like a sore tongue, weakness, or tingling in the hands or feet. Contact your healthcare provider if these occur. Low Magnesium Levels (Hypomagnesemia): Prolonged use or concurrent use with other medications that lower magnesium can cause serious symptoms like seizures, dizziness, muscle spasms, or changes in heart rhythm. Stop the medication and contact your healthcare provider if these symptoms arise. Bone Loss and Fractures: Long-term or high-dose use may increase the risk of bone loss and fractures, particularly in older adults. Storage: Store dexlansoprazole at room temperature (68°F to 77°F or 20°C to 25°C). Missed Dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take double or extra doses. Overdose: In case of an overdose, seek immediate medical attention by calling 911 or contacting a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. Dexlansoprazole is a valuable treatment for managing acid-related conditions, but it must be used responsibly under the guidance of a healthcare provider. Always communicate openly with your provider about your health and any concerns regarding this medication.
